posts.title: Wizarding World 2026 - Rumors & Discussion
posts.text: Yeah, if the Azkaban rumour is legit then it makes the most sense to see it in the vein of other "dark" locations like Grimmauld Place, the Ministry (the original playset), Malfoy Manor, and maythe the Lovegood House. Which gives us a range of EUR 100-150, and the knowledge that the bigger the building, the more it will resemble a flat facade. Azkaban unlike Malfoy Manor is just narrow and tall (similar to the Lovegood House) so it would hopefully be less facade-like. They also tend to "childify" those dark locations by either including "humourous" scenes (like with the Weasleys at Grimmauld Place) or making up bizarre interiors (i.e. the throne-like loo at Malfoy Manor, and Narcissa wrestling a giant lobster in the kitchen, while there's no inclusion of the canonical prisoner dungeons). They're even doing the latter across other themes (Barad-Dur over at LotR has an Orc cafeteria, and the Death Star over at SW has a hot tub for Stormtroopers). So I'd expect something in that vein.

posts.title: Wizarding World 2026 - Rumors & Discussion
posts.text: I mean sure it’s possible for Lego to do those rooms but they aren’t exactly the most exciting room. Rita’s room is a dusty broom closet and the trophy room is only really infamous for the meme. Not much for play features for both and not much of the story happens in those spots. Especially in comparison to the Yule Ball, which has already been made by LEGO and LEGO loves revisiting familiar locations. I find the Yule Ball far more likely, while it will be likely $280, it’s still a toy afterall. Snape’s Storeroom I could see as it has plot implications, especially if Moody’s Office is included and you could recreate the story of Barty sneaking brew or Snape accusing Harry. Tbh while I would prefer the Yule Ball I’m really down for anything, the Prefect’s Bathroom and Astronomy Classroom I think to me is the most essential so as long as they have those I’m good. I’m just happy the line is continuing.

Then there’s the Prefects’ Bathroom and Mad-Eye’s office like you mentioned – but there’s also the Trophy Room (where the champions go after selection in the movie), Snape’s Storeroom/Office, and as @JS038 mentioned, Rita Skeeter and her ‘interview room’ have the possibility of showing up too. Keeping in mind that the Astronomy Tower will be narrower than the Grand Staircase Tower and the portion that will actually accommodate rooms isn’t any higher despite the structure technically being taller, then it’s pretty easy to fill things up without resorting to shoving in things that belong in the Great Hall.

posts.title: [MOC] Danish Rubber Noses - An Ongoing Saga
posts.text: Thank you for all your nice comments! 😭 Yes! Even 36 years after entering service, the IC3 DMU (And partly the IR4 EMU) is still the backbone of Danish long distance train services. They were supposed to retire now, but with another delay of the IC5 which was supposed to enter service this year, the IC3's will probably still be around for a while. I'm probably biased, as this is a train I've seen all my life, but I love the design! I don't see it as ugly at all! This is the train that pops into my head when I think of a passenger train in general. Every Dane probably thinks this, and either knows it by the name "IC3" or simply just as a "DSB train". Thank you! The rubber nose is definitely the part of the train that I am the most proud of 😊 Joining BSBT 2026 was an awesome experience! We all got to meet so many of the great builders whose models we already knew from forums like this and Flickr. it was a lot of fun driving around between so many other nationalities, and seeing the visitors recognizing the train and taking photos/videos. Haha, that would be the next step! Though, probably not possible to do "legally" with the parts selection available at the moment. I saw someone who did an IC3 MOC where they used technic tube for the rubber front, probably to mimic the air-filled rubber hose, but I don't think it looked that nice... (Probably not helped by the fact that this build is from 2007 or earlier) By heino at Brickshelf.com And ending off with another shot of my IC3 train and IR4 train coupled together, just because :)) More photos on my Flickr account

posts.title: Wizarding World 2026 - Rumors & Discussion
posts.text: Y’know, when I said we should start getting leaks on the summer wave soon yesterday, I wasn’t expecting this soon. Another leak reporting the Astronomy Tower (and seemingly confirming we will have two castle systems going at once) is exciting. GoF wouldn’t have been my choice for that section, but given the very limited in castle options for that movie, it looks like we’ll be seeing the prefects’ bath and trophy room at the very least, and I do think those will turn out well in this system. Azkaban is a little baffling though. Sure, it’s one of the few places that haven’t been done in Harry Potter Lego, but that’s because to do the triangular monolith building shown in OotP at a scale even close to being compatible for minifigures would require a pretty steep price – and between the dark subject matter, lack of main characters, ridiculously short time on screen, and at least half the included minifigs being dementor repeats, I’m just not sure how many people would be willing to pay for that. What I could see Lego doing is testing the waters on how popular Azkaban is by doing it as a second installment of sorts in the mini buildings line after the $40 Hogwarts we got this year. I doubt we’ll see Myrtle in the prefects’ bathroom. Yes, she appears in the scene – but Nick was an iconic part of the first Great Hall scene and didn’t show up there in anticipation for pairing him with the Gryffindor common room the next year, and Quirrel is kinda the whole point of the trio facing the forbidden corridor challenges and he doesn’t show up in the Grand Staircase Tower because he’d already shown up in the Great Hall. The designers just don’t seem to want to repeat minor characters in the large castle sets for this system. I also wouldn’t expect another Yule Ball castle section. The ball happens in the Great Hall and simply doesn’t fit anywhere else. Lego only got away with putting it with another section of the castle back in 2019 by having everything about the ball be a side build completely separate from the set’s actual castle.

posts.text: Patience, Evan, patience—no need to use all capital letters. I am "almost" there; currently my 4.5V/12V trains from 1973(!) onwards are remotely controlled via LEGO Blockly. Their original motors, that is - using "slightly modified" PF receivers. As you know, LEGO Blockly can not only do PF IR (and now even 433 MHz RF PF, as per my “suggestion” to Yves), but also readily control multiple Int.A and Int.B. And almost all the "rest" of LEGO interfaces/PBricks. I am currently trying to figure out what to do with my Int.A's. There are soo many options. Stocked up 4.5V motors and cables; I just need additional sensors. Although, as I am not a purist, I really want to exploit Int.A's absolutely stunning handling of signal changes (on different DC biases—it does not care about DC; it sees changes). All work in mental progress. It is ashamed that TLG never introduced further sensors for Int.A Have a very nice weekend + all the best Thorsten

posts.text: And THAT IS FUN to do! It is so nice to see my 4.5V steam train, which was released in 1972, steaming on when pulling a LEGO Blockly slider up! A 2026 programming environment acting as a client to a powerful modern microcontroller, which sends out, with the help of a 15-year-old LINX 433 Mhz transmitter and receiver, data to a pimped PF receiver from 2010 (the code says), which in turn turns on a 4.5V train motor - with PF PWM. I'd say this is playing across multiple themes and generations of technology. I simply love that. Best Thorsten

posts.text: That is so true! However, the MPLab X IDE or the VSCode plugin from microchip is still good for programming and flashing the smallest PICs, e.g. my beloved PIC12F508 - and they still sell it! Back to the 433 MHz technology of more than two decades ago! OK, I used a "modern" version of the LINX TXM433 module, the TXM-LR series. LINX is not LINX anymore, as it has been acquired by TE Connectivity (I believe it was around 2022), but they still develop RF modules! And all major distributors (Farnell etc.) still have the good old TXM and RXM modules for sale. So, I am totally UP-TO-DATE!!! Here is the thing: I have 8 LEGO trains running on RF-PF, as my layout is mostly behind stuff, where IR never gets :D. There are: #181 4.5V Steam Train (PF receivers run fine on 4.5V!), #727 12V Diesel Locomotive, #7740 12V Intercity Train (PF receivers also run fine on 12V), and then 5 more "modern" 9V trains like #4512 (PF receivers also run fine on 9V), and PF retrofitted trains like the #12219 Maersk cargo train. They all have RF receivers plugged in and I simply don't want to change that to BLE or the like ;) Even better: IT ALL WORKS!!! My trains respond nicely (as per today) to LEGO Blockly using PF blocks. Here is the little 433MHz extension for the LEGO Blockly ESP32 PFIR server (range is about 10 m, more than enough in my attic ;) @Bliss: The flashing (version V8) is absolutely comfortable! Thank you so much for all you have done (for me, as I believe there are no further 433MHz LEGO PF users :) All the best, Thorsten

posts.text: But often, these micro antennas on ESP32-C3, S3 mini boards, they don't reach very far... With an original ESP32 (WROOM) like ESP32 Devkit 1 , the built-in antenna is much stronger. The ESP32-C3 is cheaper but has only one core, the ESP32-S3 has 2-core but a bit more pricey but still affordable. They are perfect for BLE bridges (They don't do BTC (Classic BlueTooth)) I have to try to compile the BLE Bridges to an ESP32-S3... (PF IR Bridge, and the Cubes Bridge too) I would also consider the use of M5Stack ecosystem in a lego project like the ATOM Lite that is lego 3 X 3 X 1 dimension (And I think it has a built-in IR TX Led), also the M5StickC plus that has internal battery and has built-in IR-TX Led, a small TFT screen and much more... posts.text: "Revolution" I've written before how a locomotive can lie in thought or memory for untold lengths of time, virtually dormant, and then reappear with a strong and captivating force. For me, the Nickel Plate Road 700s are one such example. This is another. Normally I would wax poetic over my connection to a railroad - and I certainly could do that here. That story, however, is better suited for a later date. While part of the connective story is not relevant, what is relevant is the present evolution of my modeling mentality: mainline steam freight railroading. This is a trend that started in earnest in 2022 during the development of 763. With a penchant for the 1940's specifically (in more ways than just Lego), I enjoy representing history. This was the era in which steam was beginning to take its final form in the United States. Steam's finest hour - the core of my modeling. Enter the Cotton Belt Route. The St. Louis Southwestern was a railroad that, as I've described in jest, seemed to enjoy throwing a Consolidation at any problem until a solution was found. They had plenty, along with ten-wheelers and other small motive power. They did roster two breed of 4-8-2, which were secured secondhand from the Florida East Coast and Rock Island to supplement passenger and freight service respectively. The Cotton Belt management, cognizant of the ideas of both efficiency and physical plant, presented the Baldwin engineers with their situation: a new, efficient, more powerful class was needed. The Baldwin engineers returned two proposals: #62784 and #62948. The latter was the winner, and a derivative thereof was ultimately chosen. The first 4-8-4 came to the Cotton Belt in September 1930. Rated for a mere 18% more tractive effort over the latest consolidation from seven years prior, the 800s were capable of handling 30% more tonnage and higher speed. These new engines got the job done. This is perhaps an understatement, as the railroad placed an order for five build-your-own copies to be assembled in their Pine Bluff shops, and included provision for various upgrades over the original Baldwins. The Cotton Belt repeated this internal order in 1942 - and finally our star enters the story. 819 was assembled in late 1942 and early 1943 - the boiler coming from Baldwin, and the shop forces taking five to six weeks to put everything together. 819, the last and largest locomotive built in Arkansas, first ran on February 8, 1943 - a war baby through and through. With such a fascinating backstory, I wish there was more to say about the service life of 819 specifically, but we can safely assume a successful career. These engines ran farther across the system as it was upgraded to handle them, initially running between Tyler and Pine Bluff, then expanding to Shreveport and East St. Louis. The 800s are known for handling the famed Blue Streak Merchandise freight trains, and for handling bridge traffic from the Southern Pacific through Corsicana, including perishables. These details are best told by David Morgan in the November, 1949 issue of Trains Magazine. Strapac's book on Cotton Belt motive power also makes specific note of the railroad using their 800s to handle wartime oil traffic, keeping same off the Gulf and thus less vulnerable to U-boat attacks. As the curtain fell for steam across the country, a handful of L-1s found delayed retirement working for the Southern Pacific. 819 was not among them. The railroad donated the swan song of the Pine Bluff Shops to the city that built it, and the engine became a static park fixture on July 22, 1955. This was not the end. In the Summer of 1982, conversations began between interested parties regarding a new future for 819 - including Cotton Belt employees. This renewed interest, combined with 66 original blueprints for the L-1 gathered from a former Cotton Belt Road Foreman of Engines, led to the creation of the Cotton Belt Railroad Historical Society, which held its first meeting in October 1983. posts.title: [App] moldqueen - Control Mould King BLE building-block toys (Android, Linux, ESP32)
posts.text: Hey folks, today I found an interesting project in the internet: "moldqueen". The app is open source and allows for connecting MK receivers to an Android Device Application - additionally the stack can be run on linux or even os ESP32. I would believe that piece of software might get very interesting for some scenarios - having an ESP32 for communicating with different Trains- and allowing one to have the controls lightweight on the smartphone. (it is interesting that the USB ports of the RasperryPi also seem to have a subset of USB-Ports on them... the digital version of a hand with 7 fingers, I reckon.. *giggle) Frontpage: https://jrichter24.github.io/moldqueen/ Github Code: https://github.com/jrichter24/moldqueen Features Open Source Multi-Hub Support (MK 4.0, MK 6.0, since version 1.2 both can also be mixed, linkie) Supporting Bluetooth Controllers (PS5, XBOX, others) Multi Radio /Device Support Android App RasperryPi / Linux / Docker container ESP32 Server/Client architecture Screenshot (2026-10-23) from the site with a matrix of the currently working components / devices: I have personally not yet tested the software - I just wanted to ask if others stumbled across the project already and may be able to hand some experiences. Overall it seems quite interesting and I may start testing around a bit in the next days. Edit: Posting in the "Digital LEGO" forum felt somehow wrong.. so I posted it to the Alt bricks forum - hope this is fine, if not please somebody state where to put.

posts.title: [MOC] Mini 42129 - Mercedes-Benz Zetros Trial Truck
posts.text: In the rear axle, the gear selector is put parallel with the axle, so in order to transmit it back to the chassis, it has to go through a perpendicular mesh, which offsets the rotation by 45 degrees. However, the axle from the gear selector in the chassis is 90 degree upright. Hence, that part 4615 is used to offset two ends of the axle that locks the differentials by 45 degrees on the same line.
